newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodia PM denies Khmer Rouge holding hostages.
newsitem.headline: Cambodia PM denies Khmer Rouge holding hostages.

text.p: Cambodian co-Premier Prince Norodom Ranariddh on Friday denied reports that 15 of his party officials were being held hostage by Khmer Rouge hardliners.

"They are not hostages," he told reporters at a tobacco company's media conference, contradicting Thursday's assertion by co-Premier Hun Sen that the missing team had been abducted by hardliners near their base at Anlong Veng on the Thai border.
The conflicting information from the co-premiers comes amid tensions between them over defections from the Khmer Rouge, which led the brutal 1975-1979 regime headed by Pol Pot.

Ranariddh and Hun Sen have both been trying to gain the upper hand in winning over defectors since the Maoist guerrilla movement began crumbling last August and continue to differ over how to handle the group.

The result is more confusion over the fate of the team from Ranariddh's FUNCINPEC party, which one week ago flew by helicopter into an area near Anlong Veng in hopes of recruiting defectors, including feared one-legged commander Ta Mok.
The team never returned from its mission.
Officials have travelled daily to the Thai border to meet with hardline rebels since the incident, but while the trips yielded about 150 Khmer Rouge defectors on Monday, no others have followed.
Some fear the missing team is being used to win leverage in negotiations for further defections.

But Ranariddh insisted: "We are in touch with Anlong Veng. "We are not negotiating about them (the 15 party officials), they are negotiating about...the hardliners, on what conditions they would join the Royal Government."

The Khmer Rouge, whose regime left more than one million Cambodians dead from murder, malnutrition, overwork and disease, signed a U.N.-sponsored peace pact in 1991 but later reneged on the deal and have been fighting the coalition elected in 1993.
Fewer 2,000 fighters are believed to remain in Anlong Veng, including Ta Mok, whose possible defection has raised the spectre of a royal amnesty for the man known as "the butcher".
Hun Sen said on Thursday he was against granting amnesty to notorious leaders such as Ta Mok, calling the September amnesty of breakaway Khmer Rouge leader Ieng Sary an exceptional case.
